sculpture.name: sculpture
sculpture.title: sculpture
sculpture.reason: Painted wooden carving of a sisiutl (double-headed serpent, here showing one head with tongue, dorsal fin, and body) is a classic Kwakwaka'wakw crest/ritual image used on house fronts, screens, and regalia. Museum credits it directly to Kwakwaka'wakw makers.

sculpture.name: figure
sculpture.title: figure
sculpture.reason: A carved wooden figure of a zoomorphic being (bear-like) holding a human figure, consistent with Northwest Coast ceremonial/crest sculpture attributed to the Kwakwaka'wakw.

sculpture.name: figure
sculpture.title: figure
sculpture.reason: A finely carved wooden figure of a seated woman with cedar-bark skirt, plaited hair, and childhood head-flattening — all features consistent with Northwest Coast (Kwakwaka'wakw) carving traditions and material culture.

household.name: fish-trap
household.title: fish-trap
household.reason: A woven cedar-bark and twig basketry fish trap, a well-documented Northwest Coast fishing technology attributed to the Kwakwaka'wakw, consistent with traditional material culture of this people.

household.name: dish
household.title: dish
household.reason: This is a carved, canoe-shaped feast dish with visible wood grain, a classic Northwest Coast (specifically Kwakwaka'wakw) serving vessel used for potlatch feasts, consistent with the claimed culture despite the category being mislabeled as ceramic.

household.name: bowl
household.title: bowl
household.reason: This is a carved alder-wood bowl, canoe-shaped with brass stud decoration and knifework, a classic Northwest Coast vessel form used by the Kwakwaka'wakw and neighboring groups; it is not ceramic (wrong category) but clearly belongs as a wooden household vessel.

household.name: spoon
household.title: spoon
household.reason: A carved wooden spoon with a formline-style animal design painted in black, consistent with Northwest Coast Kwakwaka'wakw household craft; the museum notes a reasonable identification assumption but no conflicting attribution.

household.name: wedge
household.title: wedge
household.reason: A wooden wedge for splitting canoe logs, with withe binding at the head, directly attributed to Kwakwaka'wakw makers—a classic Northwest Coast woodworking tool used in canoe/plank production.

household.name: chopper; shredder
household.title: chopper; shredder
household.reason: A yew wood bark shredder/chopper with finger-hole handle, a traditional Northwest Coast tool used for processing bark for textiles, attributed to the Kwakwaka'wakw. This is a plausible, well-documented household/craft tool type for this culture.

household.name: fish-harpoon
household.title: fish-harpoon
household.reason: A bone-tipped fish harpoon with braided line, attributed to the Southern Kwakwaka'wakw, a Northwest Coast fishing tool consistent with the culture's traditional salmon harpooning technology.

household.name: mallet
household.title: mallet
household.reason: A wooden mallet with a carved head bearing what appears to be a stylized face/eye motif characteristic of Northwest Coast art; consistent with Kwakwaka'wakw carved tool traditions.

household.name: bowl
household.title: bowl
household.reason: A carved wooden feast dish in the form of a whale supported by two human figures, a classic Northwest Coast Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial feast bowl form. Material is wood, so it is misfiled as ceramic but clearly belongs to this people.

household.name: bowl
household.title: bowl
household.reason: This is a carved alder canoe-shaped bowl with opercula shell inlay and traditional root-stitch repairs, a classic Northwest Coast feast dish attributed directly to the Kwakwaka'wakw (Southern Kwakwaka'wakw) by the museum.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A carved and painted red cedar bear-form mask signed by Tom Patterson, attributed to the Kwakwaka'wakw, a Northwest Coast people known for exactly this kind of formline-painted ceremonial mask.

masks-ritual.name: tool/implement
masks-ritual.title: tool/implement
masks-ritual.reason: This is a carved wooden "slave killer" ceremonial dance club with an abalone-inlaid face representing Tsanoqun, a documented Kwakwaka'wakw dance implement type. Category is mislabeled (this is a ritual/dance object, not household).

masks-ritual.name: head-dress
masks-ritual.title: head-dress
masks-ritual.reason: This is a finely carved wooden killer-whale headdress with typical Northwest Coast formline painting (black, red, green), consistent with Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial regalia used in dance; carved dance headdresses of this type are well within the tradition. Though filed as "garment," it is worn ceremonial regalia rather than woven cloth.

masks-ritual.name: neck-ring
masks-ritual.title: neck-ring
masks-ritual.reason: The image shows a red-dyed cedar bark neck ring with plaited tassels, a well-documented Hamat'sa ceremonial regalia item made and used by the Kwakwaka'wakw.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A carved red cedar moon mask with formline painting, signed by Tony Hunt (a well-known Kwakwaka'wakw carver) — a classic Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial mask form.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A carved wooden human-face mask with mane of hair, identified as Nuhlmahl from the Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) Winter Ceremonies — a well-documented ritual object type of this culture.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: This is a classic Kwakwaka'wakw painted wood sun mask, carved with formline design (ovoids, U-forms) and radiating rays, a well-known ceremonial mask type from this Northwest Coast culture, consistent with the museum's attribution.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: The image shows a classic Dzunukwa (Wild Woman of the Woods) mask with pursed, whistling lips, fur eyebrows, and hair, a well-documented Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial mask type.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: Carved wooden mask representing Nuhlmahl (the "Wild Man"/"Bookwus"-adjacent grotesque figure) with deep-set eye sockets, exaggerated brows, and mouthpiece holes, a documented Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial mask type used in dance ceremonies; museum attributes it specifically to Southern Kwakwaka'wakw.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: Carved wooden mosquito mask with elongated curved beak/proboscis and circular eye, attributed by the museum to Kwakwaka'wakw makers, consistent with Northwest Coast ceremonial mask traditions.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A red cedar carved and painted horned owl mask, signed by a named Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwa-Guilth) carver, with classic Northwest Coast formline design — a clear ritual/ceremonial mask made and used by this people.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A wooden transformation-style mask with mechanized eyelids and mouth, painted in Northwest Coast blue/black/red conventions, matches the museum's Kwakwaka'wakw attribution; such mechanized masks are a hallmark of Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial regalia.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A carved wooden hawk face mask with black cross-hatched cheeks, red lips and eyebrows, and a curved beak touching the upper lip, consistent with Northwest Coast Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial mask carving.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: A finely twined basketry hat with painted totemic/formline designs in blue, black, red and brown, characteristic Northwest Coast Kwakwaka'wakw woven headwear worn as clothing.

garment.name: head-dress
garment.title: head-dress
garment.reason: A cedar-bark ring headdress base, consistent with Northwest Coast ceremonial headgear worn by the Kwakwaka'wakw, attributed to them directly by the museum.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Documentary photo of a Kwakwaka'wakw village on North Vancouver Island with plank houses, a painted house-front (Chief Humset's house), and canoes on the shore — a clear ethnographic scene of the claimed people's traditional built environment.

photo.name: print
photo.title: print
photo.reason: The print reproduces a photograph of a carved Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) ceremonial mask representing the mythical Galukwiwi bird, a documented ceremonial object of this people, though the image itself is a printed postcard rather than the mask itself.

photo.name: photographic print; postcard
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); postcard
photo.reason: Documentary photograph at Alert Bay of a potlatch gathering with piles of Hudson's Bay blankets and boxes, a documented Kwakwaka'wakw practice; a house-front painting is faintly visible on the building behind. This is a genuine ethnographic scene of Kwakwaka'wakw daily/ceremonial life.

photo.name: photographic print; postcard
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); postcard
photo.reason: The photograph documents three carved totem poles with bird/animal crest figures standing beside a timber building in a village setting, consistent with Kwakwaka'wakw (or closely related Northwest Coast) totem pole traditions; museum notes it as "kwakiutl (?)" but the imagery fits the claimed culture.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: Archival photograph taken at Hope Island (Kwakwaka'wakw territory) showing men, a canoe, totem poles, feast bowls, and a wool blanket displayed in front of a longhouse structure—documentary evidence of Kwakwaka'wakw daily life and material culture despite the men's possible Haida identity.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The photograph shows two carved wooden totem poles with anthropomorphic figures, consistent with Northwest Coast carving traditions such as the Kwakwaka'wakw; the image documents their material culture.

photo.name: photographic print
photo.title: photographic print (black and white)
photo.reason: The image is a photograph documenting a carved wooden Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) mask representing Nuhlmahl, used in winter ceremonial dances — a ritual object made and used by this people, photographed for documentation.

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black and white); photographic print
photo.reason: The postcard shows two Indigenous elders from Vancouver Island seated before a timber building, a documentary portrait consistent with Kwakwaka'wakw or a closely related Vancouver Island First Nation; the region and dress are plausible even though the specific ethnic label cannot be confirmed beyond "Native Indians, Vancouver Island."

photo.name: postcard; photographic print
photo.title: postcard (black and white); photographic print
photo.reason: Documentary postcard photo of a Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) man and his wife in a traditional dugout canoe at Quatsino, showing dress and canoe craft, consistent with the claimed people and location.

instruments.name: drum; drum-stick
instruments.title: drum; drum-stick
instruments.reason: This is a hand drum with drumstick, painted with a Namgis (Kwakwaka'wakw) sun face design by named artist William Wasden Jr., a well-known Kwakwaka'wakw carver/painter — a clear match for the claimed people and category.

instruments.name: rattle
instruments.title: rattle
instruments.reason: This is a carved wooden bird-form (Thunderbird) rattle with black-and-red formline painting, a ceremonial instrument type long used by Kwakwaka'wakw and neighboring Northwest Coast peoples; nothing here contradicts the Kwakwaka'wakw attribution.

instruments.name: whistle
instruments.title: whistle
instruments.reason: A small bone whistle bound with sinew/gut thread, explicitly documented as made by Kwakwaka'wakw for use at feasts—a plausible traditional instrument type for this Northwest Coast people.

arms.name: tool/implement; club
arms.title: tool/implement; club
arms.reason: A stone club with a carved face (haliotis shell eyes, bark cord through the mouth) and wedge-shaped striking end, a well-documented Northwest Coast Kwakwaka'wakw weapon type ("slave killer" club) directly attributed by the museum.

arms.name: weapon
arms.title: weapon
arms.reason: A grey stone chisel-like weapon with a carved frog in relief, a form consistent with Northwest Coast stone weapons/implements attributed to the Kwakwaka'wakw.

arms.name: bow
arms.title: bow
arms.reason: The image shows a wooden bow with a leather-wrapped grip and gut cord, consistent with a Kwakwaka'wakw-made hunting weapon; museum attributes it "probably" to this group with no contrary evidence.

arms.name: club; fishing equipment
arms.title: club; fishing equipment
arms.reason: A wooden fish club with a carved human face head in Northwest Coast style, an object type used by Kwakwaka'wakw and neighboring peoples for dispatching fish; the record only describes it as "southern Northwest Coast style" without independent attribution evidence, but this is a widely-shared regional tool form consistent with the claimed group.

jewelry.name: bracelet
jewelry.title: bracelet
jewelry.reason: The image shows a silver repoussé bracelet engraved with an eagle design in Northwest Coast formline style, consistent with Kwakwaka'wakw silversmithing traditions and matching the museum's attribution.

jewelry.name: arm-band
jewelry.title: arm-band
jewelry.reason: The image shows two plaited red cedar bark arm bands with red cotton ties, used as Hamat'sa ceremonial regalia by the Kwakwaka'wakw, matching the claimed ethnicity and object.

jewelry.name: anklet
jewelry.title: anklet
jewelry.reason: The image shows two plaited red cedar bark ankle-bands with cotton fabric ties, used as part of Hamat'sa ceremonial regalia — a documented Kwakwaka'wakw ceremonial object.

jewelry.name: bracelet
jewelry.title: bracelet
jewelry.reason: The image shows a copper cuff bracelet with incised diagonal ridge patterning, consistent with Northwest Coast copper working traditions attributed to the Kwakwaka'wakw, an item worn as personal adornment.
